title: Seneca: life is long enough
hook: Seneca argues we are not given a short life but make it short by wasting it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cato's last night, a hard story told honestly. Your line was reach out before morning. That line stays true every night. Day thirty.
screen: `CATO'S LAST NIGHT — REACH OUT BEFORE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Everyone says it. Where did the year go? I don't have time. Life is short. Almost two thousand years ago, a Roman writer looked at that complaint, one of the oldest in the world, and said: no. I don't think that's true. His name was Seneca. Born in Spain, raised in Rome, a Stoic philosopher, a playwright, a senator, and, awkwardly, one of the richest men in the empire and the adviser to the emperor Nero. A complicated man. And he wrote a short essay, still read today, called On the Shortness of Life. Today's word is Seneca.
screen: `WHERE DID THE YEAR GO?` → `A ROMAN SAYS NO.` → `ON THE SHORTNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Seneca starts with the complaint itself. Most people, he says, even great thinkers, grumble that nature is stingy, that life runs out just as we're getting ready to live it. Then he turns it over. It isn't that we're given a short time, he argues. It's that we waste a great deal of it. Life is long enough, and generous enough, for the greatest things, if the whole of it is well spent. But when it's poured out on distractions, on chasing things that don't matter, on other people's errands we never chose, then at the end we notice it's gone, without ever having noticed it passing. His picture is money. Hand a fortune to a careless owner, and it's gone in no time. Hand a modest amount to a careful one, and it grows. Life, he says, works the same way. In his own Latin, the line is short enough to remember: vita, si uti scias, longa est. Life, if you know how to use it, is long. Now, the awkward part, because Seneca is a complicated guide. Critics in his own time pointed out that a man this rich, this close to power, was lecturing everyone else about what matters. He knew it, and wrote back that he was describing the good life, not claiming he'd reached it. You can take that as honesty or as an excuse. Either way, the essay has outlived the argument. Notice what he isn't saying. He isn't saying cram more in, be more productive. He's saying the opposite. Stop giving your life away to things you never chose, and you'll find you have more of it than you thought.
screen: `THE OLDEST COMPLAINT.` · `NOT SHORT, BUT WASTED.` · `A FORTUNE IN CARELESS HANDS.` · `A COMPLICATED GUIDE.` · then, large: `LONG ENOUGH, IF USED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then gently look back over today, or yesterday. Find one hour you gave away without really choosing to. Scrolling, a meeting you didn't need, a worry you replayed, a show you didn't even like. No guilt. Just count it. One hour. Then imagine you had it back. What would you have done with it? Let one answer come. The bell holds the time.
Seneca. A rich, complicated Roman Stoic who argued that life isn't short, only wasted.
Your line: long enough, if used. Today, count one hour you gave away. Just notice where it went. Tomorrow, Seneca shows us how to keep the books. Day thirty.

howItsDone: Many people who follow Stoic practice review their day each evening, as Seneca described doing, noticing where their time and attention actually went.

original.script: vita, si uti scias, longa est
original.say: WEE-tah, see OO-tee SKEE-ahs, LON-gah est
original.note: Latin, from Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 2.1: life, if you know how to use it, is long.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old Roman telling people life is short.
what it means: a complicated man arguing life is long enough, if it isn't wasted.
what a scholar hears: De Brevitate Vitae 1–2, addressed to Paulinus; his reply to charges of hypocrisy is in On the Happy Life 17–18.

sources.ref: On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae) 1–2
On the Happy Life (De Vita Beata) 17–18
Tacitus, Annals 13.42 (Suillius's attack on Seneca's wealth)

notes: De Brevitate Vitae 1: paraphrased (Basore 1932 not on the public-domain list). The money image is from ch. 1.
Latin 'vita, si uti scias, longa est' (2.1); some editions read 'Vita, si uti scias, longa est'. Confirm; it appears as a Latin original, not a translation.
Seneca's wealth and critics: Tacitus Annals 13.42 (Publius Suillius); Seneca's reply in De Vita Beata 17–18 ('I am not a wise man'). Confirm the summary.
Seneca born c. 4 BCE in Corduba (Spain); confirm.
